input.content:
Your team ships every week, but nobody outside the repo can tell.

That is what a changelog fixes. Not release notes for customers, not a marketing beat — a plain, dated list of what changed and why. I started keeping one three years ago on a small side project, and it quietly turned into the single most useful document I own.

Three takeaways from doing it consistently:

1. Write it the day of the change, not the day of the release. Memory rots fast, and "why" is the part that disappears first. Capture the reason while it still feels obvious.

2. Optimize for the reader who joins in six months. They will not read your commits. They will read one file. Make that file kind to them.

3. A changelog is a thinking tool, not a paperwork tool. Forcing yourself to describe a change in one sentence exposes half-baked decisions before they ship.

The compounding value is real, and the cost is a few minutes a week.

What is the smallest habit that has quietly paid off the most in your work?
